evidenceAudit.scope: Severe malaria in adults, children and pregnancy in India: recognition by WHO criteria, pre-referral treatment, parenteral artemisinin or quinine, area-specific follow-on artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT), primaquine and supportive care, built on the National Drug Policy on Malaria (NVBDCP, 2013).
findings: Parenteral artesunate 2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12 and 24 hours then daily, artemether, arteether (adults only), quinine 20 mg/kg loading then 10 mg/kg 8-hourly at no more than 5 mg/kg/hour, follow-on ACT-SP or ACT-AL, quinine follow-on with doxycycline or clindamycin, primaquine 0.75 mg/kg on day 2, use of artemisinins in all trimesters for severe malaria, and the list of things not to give checked against the National Drug Policy on Malaria 2013 (pp. 6–11).
Severe malaria criteria from WHO 2021 (via McMaster table); children under 20 kg artesunate 3 mg/kg from MSF guidance; rectal artesunate pre-referral from the WHO information note (2017).
unverifiedSections: The 2013 national policy says parenteral treatment for at least 24 hours on p. 10 and at least 48 hours on p. 11; both are shown.
The 3 mg/kg artesunate dose for children under 20 kg is from MSF and WHO, not the 2013 national policy, which gives 2.4 mg/kg without an age split.
Supportive-care doses (dextrose, anticonvulsants, transfusion thresholds) are not in the national policy; use the Hypoglycaemia and Status epilepticus topics.
Primaquine 0.75 mg/kg single dose follows the 2013 national policy; later WHO guidance uses 0.25 mg/kg. Check current NCVBDC policy.
Drug cautions, contraindications and renal or hepatic adjustment lines without a source tag are general pharmacology statements and need formulary confirmation.

pathophysiology.summary: Severe malaria is a medical emergency, usually from Plasmodium falciparum, though P. vivax can also cause severe disease in India. Parasitised red cells stick to small-vessel endothelium, blocking flow in the brain, kidneys and gut, while haemolysis and inflammation cause anaemia, acidosis and organ failure. Death can follow within hours. Parenteral artesunate is the treatment of choice; after at least 24 hours of parenteral treatment and once the patient can swallow, a full 3-day area-specific ACT is given (National Drug Policy 2013). Children under 6 years who cannot reach injectable treatment within 6 hours can be given rectal artesunate before referral (WHO 2017).
keyMechanisms: Parasitised red cells adhere to microvascular endothelium (sequestration).
Microvascular obstruction causes cerebral malaria, acute kidney injury (AKI) and lactic acidosis.
Haemolysis and splenic clearance cause severe anaemia and jaundice.
Parasite glucose consumption, quinine-induced insulin release and liver failure cause hypoglycaemia.

symptoms: Inability to sit, stand or feed (prostration)
Breathlessness, dark urine, reduced urine output
physicalSigns: Glasgow Coma Scale below 11 in adults (WHO)
Capillary refill above 3 seconds or systolic BP below 80 mmHg (WHO)
redFlags: Any WHO severity feature: treat as severe malaria at once
precipitants: Delayed or no treatment of falciparum malaria
Young children, pregnant women and non-immune travellers

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Neck stiffness; may coexist; lumbar puncture once stable.
Plasma leakage and low platelets; malaria test negative.
Exposure history, eschar, myalgia; specific tests.
Step-ladder fever, relative bradycardia; blood culture.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Glasgow Coma Scale below 11 in adults.
Base deficit above 8 mEq/L, bicarbonate below 15 mmol/L or lactate above 5 mmol/L.
Hb below 7 g/dL or haematocrit below 20% with parasitaemia above 10,000/µL.
Creatinine above 3.0 mg/dL (265 µmol/L) or urea above 20 mmol/L.
Bilirubin above 3.0 mg/dL with parasitaemia above 100,000/µL.

ruleIn.expectedFinding: P. falciparum or P. vivax; parasitaemia above 10% is severe
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Send the slide with the patient at referral (National Drug Policy).

clinicalManagement.title: Pre-referral
actions: Do RDT and smear; send case sheet, treatment history and slide with the patient (National Drug Policy p. 10).
Give a parenteral artemisinin derivative or quinine before referral (National Drug Policy p. 10).
Child under 6 years, no injectable and referral over 6 hours: single rectal artesunate 10 mg/kg (WHO 2017).

clinicalManagement.title: Parenteral antimalarial
actions: Artesunate IV or IM at 0, 12 and 24 hours, then daily (National Drug Policy p. 10).
Continue parenteral treatment for at least 24 hours (p. 10) or 48 hours (p. 11) and until the patient can take orally.

clinicalManagement.title: Supportive care
actions: Do not give corticosteroids, IV mannitol, heparin or adrenaline; avoid mefloquine in cerebral malaria (National Drug Policy p. 11).
Manage convulsions, AKI and anaemia in a high-dependency or intensive care unit (ICU).

clinicalManagement.title: Complete treatment
actions: Full 3-day area-specific ACT plus single-dose primaquine on day 2 (National Drug Policy p. 10).
After quinine: oral quinine to complete 7 days plus doxycycline or clindamycin (p. 10).

clinicalManagement.title: Pregnancy
actions: Severe malaria in any trimester: artemisinin derivatives; they do not worsen hypoglycaemia as quinine can (National Drug Policy p. 11).

medicationPlan.note: Doses are from the National Drug Policy on Malaria 2013 (NVBDCP); paediatric artesunate (3 mg/kg under 20 kg) from MSF and rectal artesunate from WHO 2017. India-only topic; the Saudi topic is unchanged. Not clinically reviewed.

learningObjectives: Recognise severe malaria by WHO criteria.
Complete treatment with the right area-specific ACT.
keyPoints: Artesunate 2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12, 24 hours (3 mg/kg under 20 kg).
Rectal artesunate 10 mg/kg pre-referral for under-6s.
ACT-SP outside the north-east; ACT-AL in the north-east.
No steroids, mannitol, heparin or adrenaline.
pitfalls: Stopping after parenteral therapy without an oral ACT.
